note: The Drowned Court's own library, and the argument the main quest is about. game/data/quests/mainline.json registers `for: [book_for_the_ninth_clause, book_the_seventh_recension]` and `against: [book_against_the_ninth_clause, ...]` and Q-MAIN-05 / Q-MAIN-09 name three of these as `revealed_by` sources of channel `book`. Until now those references pointed at nothing. Nothing here adjudicates: the mandate registry's own `adjudication_audit` says no book states whether the ninth clause is genuine, and none of these does. The three Tally volumes are one multi-volume series (RI-LOR03 §2, ≥3 series) and they diverge across volumes, because the hand in the margins does. — W1-READABLES added the TENTH volume (the leaves either side of the thirty-ninth year, where the return column stops being level, with the licence-roll date in the archive's note at the back), the APPENDIX (what was measured of previous readers after the tasting) and the SEVERANCES, and gave the fourth volume the `knowledge_key` Q-MAIN-06 had been naming at it since the quest was written. Q-MAIN-06, Q-MAIN-13 and Q-MAIN-30 name these four as `deceit.revealed_by[].source` of channel `ledger`; before this they named nothing.

books.title: The Seventh Recension of the Drowned Tally: the Clauses, entire
books.author: copied at Soulrest by Sexton Adrusa Hleran, in the year of the second great tide
books.unreliability: A faithful copy of an older book, and its faithfulness is the whole of its argument. It does not make the argument. Someone else has to.

contradicts.on: whether the Recension has ever had nine clauses

books.text:
This copy is made whole, with nothing added and nothing left out, and the copyist has set his name to it, which is the practice, and which the reader may take for what it is worth.

THE FIRST CLAUSE. The Court keeps the count of the dead of this coast, and keeps no other count, and is owed nothing for keeping it but the bread of the chapter and the roof over the stair.

THE SECOND CLAUSE. A body is entered on the day it is received and not on the day it died, and the difference between those days is written beside it, and where the difference is not known it is written that it is not known. A count that guesses is a count that has stopped.

THE THIRD CLAUSE. What the wells give back after a burial is entered in the return column in the Court's own units, by the sexton who measured it, in that sexton's own hand, on the day it was measured. No sexton enters a return that another sexton measured. There is no reason for this clause that has been written down and it has never been broken.

THE FOURTH CLAUSE. The Court buries whoever is brought, at whatever hour, of whatever people, in whatever condition, and asks nothing about the manner of the death. A Court that asks is a Court that can be lied to, and a Court that can be lied to has a count full of lies in it.

THE FIFTH CLAUSE. No sexton may hold land, and no sexton may hold a debt against a house of this coast, and a sexton who inherits either has a season to be rid of it. The dead are brought to those who want nothing from the living.

THE SIXTH CLAUSE. The books do not leave the room. Not for a governor, not for a prefect, not for the Office, not for fire. There is a stair and there is a door and there is a hand on the door, and the hand belongs to whoever is nearest, and that is the whole of the arrangement.

THE SEVENTH CLAUSE. Where two volumes disagree, both are kept. Neither is struck. The disagreement is entered in a third place with the date on which it was noticed and the name of whoever noticed it. It is not the business of a counting house to decide which of its own books is lying; it is the business of a counting house to make sure the lie survives to be read.

THE EIGHTH CLAUSE. When a sexton dies, the last page in that sexton's hand is left as it was found, unfinished if it was unfinished, and the next hand begins on the next leaf. No hand completes another's page. No hand rules a line under it. The gap is the record.

Here the clauses end.

The copyist adds, in his own person and not in the Court's: I was set to this by the chapter because the Sixth Recension had gone soft at the fold and could not be opened without loss. I have set down eight clauses because I found eight. I am told by two sextons that there ought to be a ninth and that it concerns the failing of the tide, and I have looked at every leaf of the book I was given, including the leaves that carry nothing, and there is no ninth. I say this without an opinion about it. It may be that the Sixth had one and the fold took it. It may be that the two sextons are thinking of a different book. I am a copyist and I have copied what was in front of me, which is the only thing I am for.

books.title: That the Ninth Clause Is Old: An Answer to the Archive
books.author: Sexton Ivrenne Mour, of the chapter of Soulrest
books.unreliability: Well-argued, sincerely held, and it never once addresses the ink. She does not know about the ink.

contradicts.on: whether the ninth clause of the Ninth Recension is genuine
whether the Recension has ever had nine clauses

books.text:
It is now said openly on the stair that the ninth clause was written to fit a stranger. I have heard it said by people I eat with. I am going to answer it once, in writing, so that I do not have to answer it in the yard for the rest of my life.

The case against the clause has three legs and I will take them in the order they are usually offered.

The first leg is that the Seventh Recension has eight clauses and ours has nine. This is true and it is the weakest thing an accusation was ever built on. The Seventh has eight because Hleran found eight, and Hleran says in his own hand that he was copying a book that had gone soft at the fold and could not be opened without loss. A man who tells you his source was damaged is not a man testifying that nothing was there. He is a man testifying that he could not see. There is a difference between an absence and a hole, and every argument I have heard on the stair this season has walked straight past it.

The second leg is that the ninth clause is the only clause that speaks about the future. The other eight are procedure — how a body is entered, who measures a return, what is done with a disagreement — and the ninth alone says what will happen when the tide fails. This is offered as though a book must be all one thing. I would ask the objectors to look at the eighth clause, which is not procedure either. The eighth says the gap is the record. That is not an instruction. That is a belief about what a book is for, sitting in the middle of a list of instructions, and it has never been struck because it has never stood in the way of anything.

The third leg is the one that is actually meant and is never actually said, so I will say it. The objection is that the clause is convenient. That the Court has a mandate it cannot execute, and a tide it cannot explain, and that a clause which says the count will be read by one who is owed nothing arrives exactly when the Court would like a reader who is owed nothing. I understand the shape of this suspicion. I have felt it. And I say: convenience is not evidence. If the clause were inconvenient it would not be under examination now, and it would be no older.

What is on the other side.

The language. The ninth clause uses two words that appear nowhere else in the Recension and nowhere else in the chapter's papers since. One is the word rendered debt in the phrase holding no debt to any root, which is not the word this Court has used for debt since anyone alive was hatched; we say owing. The other is the construction of the negative, which is the older three-part form. I invite anyone who thinks a clerk of our own day wrote this to sit down and forge me a sentence in that form. I have tried, as an exercise, and I produced something that any of us would spot across a room.

The silence. If the clause were new, someone would have had to write it, and someone would have had to be told to write it, and someone would have had to copy it into the fair copies without remarking on it, and the Court would have had to keep that quiet for as long as the clause has been read at chapter. The Court cannot keep the bread order quiet. We are a dozen sextons, four undersextons and an archivist who has not liked any of us for thirty years.

And the count. This is the part I will not be persuaded out of. Whoever wrote the ninth clause knew that the tide could fail. Not that it might be interfered with, not that it could be stolen from — that it could fail, on its own, as a thing that runs down. That was not thought in this province four hundred years ago. It was not thought in this province forty years ago. We have only just thought it, and we thought it because a ledgerer added up four hundred years of our own return column and found a curve in it. If a clerk of our own day forged that clause, then a clerk of our own day was already thinking a thought that our archive did not contain until this season, and I would rather believe in an old book than in a prophet on the payroll.

I am aware that none of this proves the clause. I am not trying to prove the clause. I am trying to stop us pretending that the case against it is finished, because I have watched three of my own chapter change their minds in a fortnight on nothing but the fact that everyone else was changing theirs.

Mour, at the chapter house, in the season of the reading.

books.title: On the Ninth Clause, and What Was Done to the Fair Copies
books.author: Hosk-Vei, ledgerer of the archive under the burial stair
books.unreliability: Every fact in it is checkable and the conclusion does not follow from them. He knows that. He says so at the end and then writes the conclusion anyway.

contradicts.on: whether the ninth clause of the Ninth Recension is genuine

books.text:
I have been in this room for thirty years and I have been asked about the ninth clause upward of a thousand times. I have kept a tally of the asking, because I keep a tally of everything, and the tally is the reason I am writing this down instead of saying it again.

First, what is not in dispute, so that it cannot be said later that I invented the easy parts.

The chapter-room copy of the Ninth Recension is on eight leaves of good paper. The first ten leaves carry the eight clauses that also stand in the Seventh. The eleventh leaf carries the ninth clause and nothing else, and it is the only leaf in the book with an unruled foot. Anyone may come and look. I will hold the lamp.

The ink of the ninth clause is not the ink of the eighth. I do not say this as a scholar of inks. I say it as a man who has watched ink dry in this room in this climate for thirty years. The eighth clause has gone the brown that our ink goes when the gall is heavy and the water is Soulrest water. The ninth has stayed black at the stroke and gone grey at the tail, which is what happens when the ink is thinned. I have four other documents in this archive that behave that way and every one of them was written in my own lifetime.

The hand of the ninth clause is a chapter hand. It is not a hand I can put a name to. It is the hand our fair copies are made in, which is a taught hand, which is the point of a taught hand: it belongs to none of the hands that wrote it.

The leaf is not a replacement. The stitching is original and unbroken. Whoever wrote on the eleventh leaf wrote on a leaf that was already in the book and already blank.

That is what I know. Now here is what I think, and I want the reader to notice that I have changed rooms.

Sexton Mour has written that the clause uses old language that no clerk of our day could forge. I have read her argument three times and it is the best thing anyone has written on this. It is also, if you turn it round, an argument that the clause was copied from something. A forger who copies is not a forger who invents, and copying a sentence in the old three-part negative requires nothing but an old sentence and a steady hand, and this archive is nothing but old sentences and there is a steady hand in it every day of the week.

Mour writes that the failure of the tide could not have been known four hundred years ago. I agree with her, and I do not think it helps her. I have the return column in front of me. The curve is thirty-six years old. The eleventh leaf is, by its ink, of about that generation. Mour's argument establishes that whoever wrote the ninth clause already knew the tide was going. She reads that as proof of age. I read it as a date.

And here is the thing I have not been able to get past in thirty years, and it is not evidence and I know it is not evidence.

The seventh clause of this Court says that where two volumes disagree, both are kept, neither is struck, and the disagreement is entered in a third place with the date it was noticed and the name of whoever noticed it. That is our law about our own books and it has been kept, without exception, in every case I have found, back to the fourth volume.

The Seventh Recension has eight clauses. Ours has nine. That is two volumes disagreeing.

There is no entry. Not in the disagreement book, not in the chapter minutes, not anywhere in this room. It went unnoticed. For four hundred years, in a house that writes down the day the bread was short, its own foundational text grew a clause and not one archivist saw it.

I do not conclude from this that the clause is false. I want to say that plainly, because people will quote this paper at people and they will stop before the end of it. An absence in a record is the weakest thing in the world; I have spent my life explaining that to people who wanted a gap to mean something. All I am saying is that of the two possibilities in front of us, one requires a forgery and the other requires this Court to have failed, once, silently, at the only thing it has ever claimed to be good at.

I have been asked which I believe. I have answered upward of a thousand times that the question is not useful and I will answer it that way again. But I have written this out, and I have put it where it will be found, and a man who thought the question was not useful would not have done that.

Hosk-Vei, in the archive, which is not to be left with the door open.

books.title: The Drowned Tally, Fourth Volume: leaves ninety-one to ninety-nine
books.author: the sextons of Soulrest, and one other

series.of: the fourth of the volumes still whole

books.unreliability: A ledger cannot lie about what it entered and can be entirely wrong about what it meant. The corrections in the margin are in a hand nobody has ever met.
books.text:
Entries are as the Court makes them: the name where a name was given, the day received, the difference between the day received and the day of death where that was known, and the return measured at the well afterwards in the Court's units. Where a hand changes, the change is at a leaf.

Leaf ninety-one, in the hand of Sexton Ollo Vaen.

A man of the barge crews, no name given, received on the eleventh, dead four days. Return: nine.
A woman of Stilt-Row, Weeja-Ei, received the same day, dead one. Return: nine.
A hatchling of the rotting quarter, unnamed by custom, received the twelfth, dead the same day. Return: nine.
A Nord, name written as Halstig, received the fourteenth, dead a week, brought up the coast in salt. Return: two. Vaen notes: he was a long way from his own ground and I do not know what to make of the two, and I am entering it as I measured it, per the third clause.

In the margin, in a small even hand that is not Vaen's and is not any hand the chapter can name: the two is correct. Do not adjust it. He is not short; he is elsewhere.

Leaf ninety-three, Vaen.

Twelve of the fever, received over nine days, all of the Bone Ladder. Returns: nine, nine, nine, nine, eight, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine.

In the margin: the eighth is mine. Measured again at the turn and it stands at eight. Enter eight.

Vaen, in his own hand, below: I have measured it three times at eight and I do not know who is writing in this book. I have asked the chapter. The chapter says the marginal hand has been in the Tally since before the oldest of them was received into it, and that the corrections have never once been wrong, and that I am to leave them alone and not to speak about it to the mortuary hands because they are superstitious. I am entering eight. I want it recorded that I am entering eight because I measured eight and not because of the margin.

Leaf ninety-five, Vaen.

A long list, the winter, forty-one received.

At the foot of the leaf, in the marginal hand: the count for this leaf is correct in every line and the sum at the foot is wrong by one. The error is Vaen's and it is a copying error and not a measuring error, which are different things and this house should say which it has made.

Leaf ninety-six, Vaen, and this is the last leaf in his hand.

Three received, of the road. Returns: nine, nine, and

Here the leaf stops. Per the eighth clause no hand has completed it and no line has been ruled under it. The next leaf begins in the hand of Sexton Bela Ravano, who writes at the head of it: Vaen died on the road on the second, with the book in his bag, and the bag was brought back and the book was not opened until the chapter sat. He had entered two of the three. I have entered the third on the next leaf under my own hand and left his page as it was found, and I would ask whoever reads this in a hundred years to understand that I did not want to.

At the foot of leaf ninety-nine, in the marginal hand, the only entry it has ever made that is not a number:

I. M., Steward of the Count. I have read the whole of this volume and it is honest. That is not a compliment. An honest count is the only kind that is any use to me.

books.title: The Drowned Tally, Sixth Volume: the disputed leaves, with the archive's note
books.author: the sextons of Soulrest; the note by Hosk-Vei
books.unreliability: The volume everybody has to have an opinion about. It can be read two ways and the ledgerer says so and refuses to prefer either.

contradicts.on: the Court's unit of return and whether it has drifted

books.text:
A note from the archive, set at the front of the volume so that the reader does not get twenty leaves in before finding out what they are looking at.

This volume covers a hundred and one years and it is the volume the Court argues about, and the argument turns on no wrongdoing at all. It is about the units.

For the first sixty years of it the return is entered in ninths, which is how the Court has always measured: the well is drawn at the turn of the tide, the draw is set against the standing measure, and what comes back is written as so many parts of nine. A full return is nine. There is nothing mystical about the nine. It is the number of notches on a stick that has been in the salt-store since before the stick was worth remarking on.

For the last forty years of it the return is entered in twelfths. The why was never written down. There is no chapter minute, no note at the change of hand, nothing. On leaf two hundred and six the column says nine and on leaf two hundred and seven, in the same hand, in the same season, it says twelve, and the hand does not stop to explain itself to anyone.

Here is why it matters and here is why I will not settle it.

If the stick was recut — if a clerk at some point in the fourth century made a new standing measure with twelve notches and the house simply carried on — then a twelve in the late leaves means what a nine meant in the early ones, and the return in this volume is flat, and the whole of the sixth volume is a hundred and one uneventful years.

If the stick was not recut — if the sextons of that generation were writing the same draw against the same nine notches and had merely started calling a full return twelve for a reason of their own — then the returns in the late leaves are short, and they are short by a quarter, and the tide was already going four hundred years ago, and everything the Court believes about when this started is wrong by three centuries.

I have looked for the stick. There is a stick in the salt-store. It has nine notches and it is not old enough.

I have looked for a second stick and there is no second stick, and there is no inventory of sticks, because in four hundred years it never occurred to this house that a stick was a document.

What I can tell you is that the marginal hand — the one the Court calls the Steward of the Count, which enters corrections and enters nothing else — corrects in ninths on both sides of the change. It goes on writing nine where the sextons have started writing twelve. It does this for forty years without ever remarking on the difference, which is the single most irritating fact in this room, because it means the hand knew and did not think the house needed telling.

A reader who wants to add up the tide across four hundred years must decide what to do with this volume. I have added it both ways. I am not going to tell you which way I added it first, and I am not going to tell you what I think, and if you have come down here to be told, the door is behind you and it sticks.

books.title: The Drowned Tally, Eleventh Volume: the current leaves
books.author: Sexton Corvo Sedd, Sexton Ravel Doun, and Undersexton Bel Mourne
books.unreliability: Contemporary and therefore the least argued-over and the most likely to be wrong, since nobody has had time to find the errors.

contradicts.on: the Court's unit of return and whether it has drifted

books.text:
In use. Leaves are entered as they are filled and the volume is not bound until it is full, which is the practice for a working book and is why the corners have gone.

From the leaves of this season, in three hands.

Sedd. Fourteen received off the coast road in eight days, which is a great many for a season with no fever in it. Returns entered at four, four, three, four, four, four, three, four, four, four, four, three, four and four. I have set them against the standing measure twice each because I did not believe the first set.

Doun, on the next leaf. Sedd has asked me to enter beside his that the measure is not at fault, that he and I drew together on the fourth and the sixth and got the same, and that a return of four is now an ordinary return on this coast and has been for as long as either of us has been a sexton. I am entering that. I would add, in my own person, that I was received into this house in the old Undersexton's time and I was taught that a full return is nine and that a return under seven is written up for the chapter. I have not written one up for the chapter in four years. I stopped because the chapter asked me to stop, on the grounds that a report every week is not a report.

Mourne, at the head of a leaf, and this entry has been read out at chapter and is the reason there is an argument about it.

Eleven boxes came back from the burial ground on the ninth, in the ordinary way, to be re-used. The hands who carried them say they came back light. I have weighed three. They are the weight of an empty box. That is not remarkable; they are empty boxes. What is remarkable is that the hands wanted it written down, and that they wanted it written down in the Tally and not in the yard book, and that when I asked them why the Tally they could not tell me and would not go away.

I am entering it in the Tally. Under the fourth clause we do not ask about the manner of a death, and under the seventh we do not strike a thing because it is inconvenient, and I can find no clause that tells me what to do about eleven boxes that are the correct weight and that eleven grown men are frightened of. So it is entered. Eleven boxes, the ninth, returned light in the opinion of those who carried them, weight found ordinary by me.

The margin of this leaf is empty. I want that recorded too. In four hundred years the marginal hand has entered a correction on every leaf where a sexton was uncertain and it has entered nothing here, and I have looked at this empty margin every day for a month.

books.title: The Drowned Tally, Tenth Volume: the leaves either side of the thirty-ninth year
books.author: the sextons of Soulrest; the note on the licence roll by Hosk-Vei
books.unreliability: Every figure in it was measured by the person who wrote it and not one of them was ever set against the figure above. A book can be honest line by line and say nothing at all until somebody adds it up.
books.text:
A note from the archive, set at the front, because a reader who comes to this volume out of order will not otherwise know why it is the one every reader is sent to.

The tenth is the volume in which the return column stops being level. Nine volumes go before it and the return is nine, and nine, and nine, and an eight where a sexton was tired, for three hundred and sixty years. This one begins the same way and does not end the same way.

Leaf one hundred and two, in the hand of Sexton Corvo Sedd the elder. The year twenty-six.

Received twenty-two in the season. Returns: nine, nine, nine, nine, nine, eight, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine, eight, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine, nine.

Leaf one hundred and nine, Sedd. The year thirty-three.

Received nineteen. Returns: nine throughout, and a nine struck through and written again as nine, because I dropped the stick in the water and drew a second time to be sure.

Leaf one hundred and fourteen, Sedd. The year thirty-nine.

Received twenty-six. Returns: nine, nine, nine, eight, eight, nine, eight, eight, seven, eight, eight, eight, seven, eight, eight, eight, eight, seven, eight, eight, eight, seven, eight, eight, eight and seven.

In the margin, in the small even hand that is not Sedd's: the sevens are correct. Do not draw them again.

Sedd, under it: I have drawn them again. They are sevens. I have gone back through my own last four leaves and this is the first season in twelve years with a seven in it and there are six of them!

Leaf one hundred and twenty, Sedd. The year forty-five.

Received thirty-one. Returns run between six and eight, and the eights are the ones received in the first month.

At the foot: I have written to the chapter to ask a plain question. Has any house on this coast recut the standing measure inside my service? The chapter has written back that none has, and has asked me not to raise it at the sitting.

Leaf one hundred and thirty-one, in the hand of Sexton Bela Ravano the younger. The year fifty-two.

Received forty. Returns between five and seven. Ravano, at the foot: Sedd is dead and I have his leaves and his question. What is wrong with the stick? Nothing is wrong with the stick. I've three of them and they agree.

Leaf one hundred and forty-eight, Ravano. The year sixty-one.

Received thirty-six. Returns between four and six. In the margin, one correction, downward, in the small even hand. Ravano has written beside it: agreed, and thank you, and who are you? Under that, in a third hand, later and harder: Ravel, don't write to it!

Leaf one hundred and sixty, the last leaf of this volume. The year seventy.

Received forty-four. Returns between four and five.

The archive's note, at the back, written by me and signed, because a reader may want to know which parts of the last four pages are the book and which are the archivist.

The book is everything above. What follows is mine.

I have set this volume against the Provincial Office's licence roll, which is kept at Gideon and which I have read twice and copied once. The first licence to open a sapwell for sale was granted on the seventh day of the seventh month of the year forty-seven, and there is no earlier grant in the roll and no gap in the roll where one could have been.

The first seven in this book is in the year thirty-nine. That's eight years of daylight, and I have written it here because in thirty years I have had four readers in this room and three of them arrived certain that the cutting came first. It would be a great deal tidier if it had. The Court would like it. The Cutters would deserve it. I have looked for a way to read these two dates in the other order and there is not one.

What I will not do is add this book up for you. Eleven volumes are on that shelf and the sum is a season's work and the sixth of them can be read two ways, and a total in my hand is a total in the hand of a man who has already told you what he thinks it says. Wedge the door. The lamp oil is yours.

books.title: The Drowned Tally, the appendix bound at the back: of readers, and what was measured of them after
books.author: the archivists of Soulrest, each in turn, none of them signing
books.unreliability: The one part of the Tally that was never meant to be read by the person it is about, and it is written in exactly the same dry hand as the burials.
books.text:
Bound at the back of the current volume and moved forward each time the current volume changes. It is four leaves and it has been four leaves for four hundred years.

Entered here: every person who has been put into the Count at the seventh bay, the date of it, and what was measured of them at each re-issue afterward. The measure is the ordinary one. A re-issue that comes back as what went in is entered as nine.

  Aveline Rell the elder, the second archivist of that name. Put in on the fourth of the wet, year one hundred and ninety-one.
      first re-issue    nine
      second            nine
      third             eight and a part
      fourth            eight
      fifth             seven and a part
      sixth             seven
      seventh           six and a part
    Died between the seventh and an eighth. The chapter recorded that she had become difficult to be in a room with and was in no pain.

  Ollo Vaen the younger, sexton. Put in on the ninth of the dry, year two hundred and forty.
      first             nine
      second            eight and a part
      third             eight
      fourth            seven
    Four, and then he stopped going into the water. He lived thirty years after and is buried under the stair.

  Ixina Sheel, of the Xul-Aneekh, who came to the Court for this and for nothing else. Put in on the first of the wet, year three hundred and four.
      first             nine
      second            nine
      third             nine
      fourth            eight and a part
      fifth             eight
      sixth             seven and a part
    Six entries and no seventh. The gallery took her back and did not send word.

  Tertius Ollo, a legate's clerk, against the Court's advice and with the Court's leave. Put in on the sixth of the dry, year three hundred and fifty-one.
      first             eight and a part
    One. He wouldn't go in a second time and he was the only one of them who was told this appendix existed, because he asked, out loud, in this room, whether there was a book of the ones who had gone before him.

The archive's standing note on this appendix, copied forward by each archivist and never signed by any of them.

The cost as it is stated to a candidate is true and is complete as far as it goes: the pattern is taken, the pattern is kept, and there is no rite, no keeper, no cure and no ending in this province that takes it back out. Every archivist has said that plainly and every archivist has said it three times.

What is in this appendix is the term that is not stated. A pattern that is held in the Count comes back from a well a little further from itself each time it is drawn, and the column above is what a little further looks like when it is written down over sixty years.

Why is it not stated? Because it was stated once, to a clerk who asked, and he did not go in, and the Court needed a reader that season and did not get one.

That is the reason and it isn't a good one. Whoever is archivist when this is read out loud in front of a witness will have to say it in his own voice, and every archivist who has ever kept these four leaves has known that the day would come and has hoped to be dead first.

books.title: The Drowned Tally, the severed entries: three, with the dates
books.author: the archivists of Soulrest, in the ordinary hand
books.unreliability: Three entries written by three people who were each certain the Court would not survive theirs. The Court survived all three, which the book records and does not comment on.
books.text:
Kept as a set of three leaves, out of order with the rest, because they are read together or they are read wrong.

An entry of this kind is made when a claim under the ninth clause is severed: when the claimant is shown to have been mistaken, or when the claimant breaks the thing the clause is about, or when the claimant dies in a way that ends it. The form was set at the first of them and has not been altered.

The first. Year one hundred and twelve, the eighth of the wet.

A claimant of nine years' standing, a sexton of this house, who read the count and gave the chapter a figure and was found, by two hands working apart, to have added the fourth volume twice. The figure was withdrawn. He was not put out of the house and he did not ask to be. Entered by the archivist of the day, whose note reads: the count is wrong and the clause is not. We will need another reader and there is no rule that says the next one must be better than this one.

The second. Year two hundred and sixty-eight, the third of the dry.

A claimant who killed a rootkeeper at the fourth hollow, in an argument about a gate, in front of eleven people. The claim was severed the same season by the chapter without a vote, which is the only time that has been done. The archivist's note reads: the clause asks for a person who is owed nothing. It does not ask for a good one. The chapter has decided that it does, and I am entering the decision and not agreeing with it.

The third. Year three hundred and nineteen, the first of the wet.

A claimant who went down at the Bone Ladder and did not come up, in the second year, before anything was settled either way. Entered by the archivist of the day, whose note reads: it isn't known whether the claim was ever good. Nothing that has happened tells us. A death is not an argument and I would ask a later reader not to make it into one.

The archive's note at the foot of the third leaf, added later, in a fourth hand.

Three in four hundred years, and the book was longer than all three of them. It went on being kept the next morning in each case, by whoever was next, and the return column did not change on any of the three days.

What a reader is to take from this: the clause was severed and the count was still there. Has the machine under the Wastes ever had an opinion about the Court's paperwork? This house cannot answer that, and none of the three entries above pretends to.

Space is left below for a fourth. It has been left below for a fourth since the third was written and the leaf has never been cut down to fit the book.
